content_en:
# Google Cloud launches Gemini for healthcare.

Google Cloud has announced Gemini for healthcare, an AI solution engineered to unify fragmented clinical, operational, and administrative systems. Moving beyond simple information retrieval, it enables healthcare teams to turn siloed data into coordinated action.

Clinicians lose nearly 28 hours each week to paperwork and administrative tasks, fueling burnout and straining budgets. By integrating specialized skills and data connectors with existing third-party systems, the platform brings together critical information from electronic health records, billing platforms, clinical guidelines, and Medicare datasets.

Gemini for healthcare reasons across this context to orchestrate and execute complex, multi-step workflows — such as medical records synthesis and prior authorization review — within defined guardrails and with appropriate human oversight. Initially available in preview alongside launch partners including HCA Healthcare, Highmark Health, and Northwell Health, it resolves bottlenecks and reclaims valuable staff time for patient care. Learn more on the Cloud blog.

content_en:
### Google enters decision model market with Gemini Decisions API

Google LLC today launched Gemini Decisions API, an artificial intelligence service designed to answer user questions in a cost-efficient manner.

It’s powered by a new AI model called Gemini Decision 1.

Traditional large language models are designed to answer a broad range of prompts. Gemini Decision 1 has a much narrower focus: It can process just three types of questions. The upside is that it answers those questions at a significantly lower cost. According to Google, the model is nearly five times cheaper than its entry-level Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite LLM.

The model can answer yes-no questions, multiple choice questions and prompts that ask it to rate an item on a user-specified scale. A cybersecurity team, for example, could ask the model to rate the severity of an antivirus alert on a scale of 1 to 10.

Gemini Decision 1 prompts include two items: the user’s questions and the dataset to which those questions pertain. The dataset can include up to 256,000 tokens worth of text, audio, images, video or some combination thereof.

LLMs usually generate verbose free-flowing text in response to user questions. Gemini Decision 1, in contrast, outputs terse answers such as “yes” or “no.” It also displays a score that indicates how confident it is in the accuracy of a given response. That score helps applications decide whether they should make use of the output.

Neural networks designed to generate brief answers to simple questions are known as decision models. The first such model, Jev, was launched in mid-September by a startup called TypeSafe AI Inc. It gained a million users within a few days. Three weeks after the launch, TypeSafe raised $870 million at a $7.5 billion valuation.

Decision models can answer the narrow set of questions for which they’re optimized faster than LLMs. Additionally, they’re easier to integrate into applications. An application that powers some of its features using an AI model must check the model’s output for errors and filter redundant details before ingesting it. Decision models’ concise, structured responses make both tasks simpler.

“Gemini Decision 1 scores options without token-by-token decoding, keeping median latency 50-100 ms of model compute (150-250 ms end-to-end), across multimodal inputs and contexts up to 16K tokens, remaining nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions per request,” Google DeepMind product manager Min Choi and principal scientist Felix Yu wrote in a blog post.

Google checked how Gemini Decision 1 compares to Jev and OpenAI Group PBC’s Decisions API, a competing service that launched last month. The search giant says that its model performed better across seven of the nine benchmarks it tested. However, Jev proved to be slightly more cost-efficient.

Gemini Decision 1 is available through the Gemini Decisions API for 10 cents per 1 million input tokens. Google doesn’t charge for output tokens. The algorithm is also accessible through a limited free tier in Google AI Studio, a service that developers can use to familiarize themselves with the search giant’s models.

content_en:
### Google’s GKE Labs turns reinforcement learning into a Kubernetes workload

Model fine-tuning through reinforcement learning is fast becoming one of the most demanding jobs in AI infrastructure. It mixes training, inference and sandboxed agent work in a single loop, often with research code tangled into the systems beneath it.

Google LLC has been tackling that problem from inside its Kubernetes engineering group, and recently donated the result, OpenRL, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. The GKE Labs team got there by building an AI agent for Kubernetes tasks, then a benchmark to grade models on that work, according to Sunil Arora (pictured, left), senior software engineer at Google Cloud.

“If you look at reinforcement learning, I think of it as a kind of a super app of AI because it involves training. It involves sampling. It involves agents actually doing things in a sandbox and sometimes kind of evaluating the work,” Arora said. “It’s kind of a very diverse workload and it is, I think, pushing the boundaries of our infrastructure.”

Arora and Justin Santa Barbara (right), developer at Google, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed model fine-tuning and their work in GKE Labs, which puts experimental projects in users’ hands early. *(\* Disclosure below.)*

### Model fine-tuning without the infrastructure tangle

OpenRL debuted as a research preview in June 2026, offering a self-hosted training API for a company’s own Kubernetes cluster. It splits the reinforcement learning loop from the compute plumbing, so infrastructure engineers handle scaling while researchers keep control of experiments, Arora explained.

“With OpenRL, one of the things that we are trying to do is kind of abstracting away the infrastructure as kind of core primitives so that researchers and AI engineers can just focus on their RL loop,” Arora said.

Sandboxes are where that loop meets agent infrastructure, since calculating rewards can mean running millions of isolated commands. Google’s Agent Substrate packs more of those sandboxes onto limited compute, according to Arora. For Santa Barbara, the need surfaced one step at a time.

“We built kubectl-ai, and in theory, kubectl-ai could have formatted my hard disk,” Santa Barbara said. “I would quite like a sandbox for this so that if it formats a hard disk, it formats that sandbox and no damage.”

title: Jensen Huang accused of having another affair — with an Nvidia exec
excerpt: Jensen Huang, who has come under fire for admitting to an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese intelligence agent, has been accused of having a separate affair with an Nvidia subordinate.
title_en: Jensen Huang accused of having another affair — with an Nvidia exec
excerpt_en: Jensen Huang, who has come under fire for admitting to an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese intelligence agent, has been accused of having a separate affair with an Nvidia subordinate.
content_en:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is already under investigation after having admitted to having an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. Now the New York Times is reporting that Huang is also suspected of having another extramarital affair, with a direct report of his at the company — Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. Powell, like Huang, is married, the outlet says.

The Times says it was told of the alleged affair by five employees at the company. The sources said that Huang and Powell were captured on video “being affectionate at a San Jose, Calif., hotel” during a conference earlier this year.

Like many companies, Nvidia has rules discouraging superiors from having relationships with employees in subordinate roles, the Times notes. TechCrunch reached out to Nvidia for comment.

The company’s board has initiated an investigation into Huang’s publicly admitted affair. Additionally, two House Republicans said Wednesday that Congress is gearing up to subpoena Huang over the spy allegations if he doesn’t voluntarily respond to their summons to a closed-door briefing. Late Wednesday, after the reports of the second affair were published, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Nvidia board was preparing to oust Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993.

content_en:
### Google tests Tabletop, letting groups build planning tools with an AI agent

Google LLC today began testing Tabletop, a Google Labs experiment in which groups share an online space and ask an artificial intelligence agent to build the planning tools they need.

In a blog post, Roman Nurik, design and engineering lead at Google Labs, wrote that coordinating a family trip or a potluck goes more smoothly when the whole group can pitch in from one place. Whoever sets up a space adds the links, files and ideas the group has collected, and from there a request to @tabletop produces the tool.

Tools Google lists include itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters and tournament brackets, and there is a set of starter templates that Tabletop users can access as well. Once the space is shared through an invite link posted in the group’s existing chat, everyone can work on those tools at the same time, “like in a Google Doc,” Nurik wrote.

When a guest at an office party in one of Google’s demos ends up seated next to the boss, a request to @tabletop turns the seating chart into one where name badges can be dragged between tables. Any tool can be reworked the same way, according to the Tabletop site.

Google did not say which of its models run Tabletop. When Labs released its Disco browser experiment last December, Gemini 3 was the model it used to turn a person’s open tabs into small web apps.

Tabletop also follows Google’s move in September to let up to six members of a household share the division’s CC agent. Rival OpenAI Group PBC added group chats to ChatGPT a year ago, and up to 20 people can now talk to the chatbot in one thread.

In ChatGPT the chatbot sits inside the conversation as one more member, and OpenAI said at launch that it had taught the model to judge when to join in. Replies in those chats initially came from GPT-5.1 Auto, which chooses a model based on the prompt and on the subscription of whoever ChatGPT is answering. OpenAI also kept personal memory out of group chats entirely.

Tabletop is limited for now to U.S. users 18 and older who sign up through the waitlist at tabletop.google, with Google saying it will let more people in each week. Google’s announcement does not mention pricing or a release outside the U.S.

title: Amazon's Ring unveils flying drone and robot to patrol homes and businesses
excerpt: Amazon's $250 Ring Drone Cam flies from room to room to investigate suspicious activity, and can capture footage at night.
title_en: Amazon's Ring unveils flying drone and robot to patrol homes and businesses
excerpt_en: Amazon's $250 Ring Drone Cam flies from room to room to investigate suspicious activity, and can capture footage at night.
content_en:
Amazon's Ring is going deeper into surveillance with an indoor drone for home monitoring and an autonomous robot designed to patrol businesses.

The company on Tuesday unveiled the $250 Ring Drone Cam, a security camera that can fly from room to room, including upstairs, as well as capture footage during the day or at night. When an alarm or sensor on windows, doors and home security devices is triggered, the textbook-sized drone travels a preset path to investigate suspicious activity. Users can also deploy the drone at any time, the company said.

At a demo in New York on Monday, Ring CEO Jamie Siminoff said the drone could be used as a home monitoring tool and as a crime "deterrent" due to the device's built-in LED lights.

"If someone is going around your house at night, and your motion detector goes off on your Ring doorbell, imagine if you see spotlights and something flying across the window," Siminoff said. "You're probably not going to go into that house."

The drone, which can fly up to eight minutes at a time before autonomously returning to its charging dock, has two plastic-encased propellers that emit a loud buzz when it's airborne.

Ring devices have provided Amazon another avenue to grow its presence in the smart home beyond its Echo smart speakers and Eero routers, expanding in a market that Grand View Research estimates will top $200 billion in sales this year. It's equally fertile ground for Amazon rivals Apple and Google.

Ring, which Amazon acquired in 2018 and is known for its doorbells, has been beset with privacy concerns, primarily due to its partnerships with police. Earlier this year, Ring faced renewed scrutiny over a controversial Super Bowl ad touting an AI pet-finding tool called "Search Party." It then canceled an integration with police tech provider Flock Safety, which has also faced widespread backlash over its automated license plate readers.

Ring first previewed its drone, then called the Always Home Cam, in 2020. Siminoff said he chose to hold off on releasing the device until Amazon could perfect the design, sensors and data processing.

The company on Tuesday also debuted the $1,000 Ring Rover Cam. The device repurposes Amazon's Astro home robot, which had a short life as a business device and has seen few upgrades since its 2021 debut, for companies to use to patrol offices, warehouses and other workspaces.

Ring said it "leveraged the best of Astro" to build the Ring Rover Cam, which it describes as a "purpose-built security robot."

Similar to the Astro, the device is a display mounted on a two-wheeled base with an extendable periscope camera. It also features a "built-in siren," two-way audio and a "light tower" that shines onto the ceiling to help users keep track of its whereabouts.

Siminoff said in an interview that the drone and the robot allow users to monitor multiple areas of their home or business with just one device.

"People like indoor cameras, but they don't necessarily want them everywhere around their home," Siminoff said.

Ring said privacy is the "default" mode for both the drone and the robot, which flash an LED light when they're recording.

Siminoff said the drone can't fly outside per Federal Aviation Administration regulations, which restrict operating drones unless they're within a line of sight of a pilot.

"We have told our customers not to do that because it's illegal," Siminoff said. "We've also put guardrails in there to make it so it doesn't fly outside."

The Ring Drone Cam ships in the U.S. on Jan. 27, pending approval from the Federal Communications Commission, while the Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping to users on Dec. 16, the company said.

title: A New AI Tool From Google DeepMind Proved the Signal Protocol Is Secure
excerpt: DeepMind researchers were able to formally verify that the widely used encryption protocol works as intended. Their stretch goal? Do the same for “all the software of the world.”
title_en: A New AI Tool From Google DeepMind Proved the Signal Protocol Is Secure
excerpt_en: DeepMind researchers were able to formally verify that the widely used encryption protocol works as intended. Their stretch goal? Do the same for “all the software of the world.”
content_en:
Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.

Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world's communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind's formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code.

More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn't have critical vulnerabilities.

Before the AI era, it was incredibly time-consuming for people to describe the characteristics of software they wanted to prove, turn these summaries into formulas, and then develop the proof. Agentic AI can significantly cut down the time of the latter project, enabling analyses like DeepMind's Signal evaluation. But even this analysis was limited in scope—it did not, for example, formally verify the entire Signal mobile app—and DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process.

“We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work.

While the speed of the project was notable, the DeepMind researchers point out that they were able to get a head start to a degree because of some past formal verification work that the Signal Foundation has conducted.

“While prior formal verification focused on smaller portions of the code, Google DeepMind's approach enables significant expansion,” Ehren Kret, Signal's chief technology officer, says in a statement. “As AI-driven security threats grow, rigorously verifying the Signal protocol implementation gives us even greater confidence in our code's privacy guarantees.”

For critical services used in high-stakes settings, it would be a dream to be able to formally verify every code base and entire software supply chains. “If you can now verify the correctness of these implementations, then you can rest easy,” says Pushmeet Kohli, chief scientist at Google Cloud and DeepMind's vice president of research. “You can imagine banks, imagine all those other companies who rely on assurances and who worry about bugs who could now say, ‘I can prove these properties.’"

The open question across the tech sector, though, is whether AI-automated formal verification can truly scale—and whether it can do so at a workable cost. DeepMind conducted the Signal analysis free of charge as a research project, and Google declined to share the cost of the analysis. The company also declined to comment on whether it has plans to release a commercial formal verification product or service.

The researchers say that some of their crucial advancements are in developing a “human-AI collaboration process,” as Chaudhuri puts it, that allows agents to contribute and self-correct at almost every phase of the process while still seeking human input and review at key junctures. “We don’t want this sort of vibe world where AI is generating the goals and AI is generating the proofs and basically taking tests that are self-written," Chaudhuri says. “There’s a middle ground.”

title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
excerpt: The affair could have ramifications for national security as the U.S. and China race to develop the most advanced AI infrastructure.
title_en: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
excerpt_en: The affair could have ramifications for national security as the U.S. and China race to develop the most advanced AI infrastructure.
content_en:
Nvidia co-founder CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in an affair that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and potentially impact national security.

United States officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.)

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company, had reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, the Times has reported.

The story took a sudden new turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up.

Separately, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang, and Nvidia’s shares fell in after-hours trading.

The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities.

As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.

### November 11, 2026: Nvidia’s stock drops as board reportedly preps to oust CEO Jensen Huang

After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per the Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days.

Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said. The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan.

#### November 11, 2026: Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him, NYT says

The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO.

According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year.

#### November 11, 2026: Congress plans to subpoena Huang to answer questions about affair

Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressman to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China committee Chairman Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed.

#### November 9, 2026: Huang pulls out of various speaking engagements

The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum.

#### November 9-10, 2026: Details emerge about the business relationships between Nvidia and the alleged spy

Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported. The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips.

Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported. Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang.

In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported.

#### November 8, 2026: Trump shows support for Nvidia CEO, calls him a “fine person”

On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO.

“I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said.

When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia, Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.”

#### November 8, 2026: Huang admits to affair in public message to Nvidia employees; Nvidia board of directors begins investigation

Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.”

“Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote.

Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day.

#### November 5, 2026: Three Republican committee chairmen ask Huang for closed-door briefing

Three Republican congressmen — Chairman John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Chairman Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Chairman Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence — sent a request to Huang for a closed-door joint briefing with their three committees.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the \[People’s Republic of China\]’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.”

#### October 29, 2026: Jensen Huang publicly revealed to have developed ‘close relationship’ with suspected Chinese spy

U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year when the New York Times broke the story in late October that the two executives also had a close relationship.

An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary.

“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.”

#### Spring 2026: A secret memo circulates in the Trump administration about Nvidia CEO’s alleged relationship with Chinese spy

U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Securit

content_en:
# Helsing built an AI system that prepares targets for weapons systems and says every decision will carry a human name

## Key Points

- Defense company Helsing has unveiled "Clarity," an AI platform that aggregates sensor feeds and reports to identify military targets and recommend weapons systems.
- Helsing emphasizes European sovereignty and mandatory human authorization for every strike, positioning itself as a competitor to US vendors like Palantir.
- Experience with similar systems reveals significant risks. In practice, human review times often shrink to just seconds, and AI errors can trigger dangerous wrong calls.

**German defense tech company Helsing has unveiled Clarity, an agent-based software platform that distills sensor data into target recommendations. Helsing promises European control and human oversight. The use of comparable systems in Iran, in Gaza, and in a near-miss involving China shows where those promises break down.**

Helsing presented its Clarity platform in Berlin on Wednesday, calling it an "agentic intelligence platform." According to the company's press release, the software processes all data a military unit can access, including sensor feeds, open-source intelligence, written reports, and systems already in use. Hundreds of specialized AI agents link these sources, identify military forces, facilities, and positions, and prepare information on adversary assets for human review before Clarity packages the data for the appropriate weapons system.

The agents are trained on real operational data, synthetic AI-generated data, and simulated environments, Helsing says, and a shared military ontology and evidence base lets them work in parallel and deploy analytical tools. The platform is "AI-native" and not built on legacy architectures, according to the company.

Helsing stresses the system's sovereignty, noting that Clarity runs on the customer's own infrastructure and that its models and interfaces were developed in Europe, with data and operations staying under the armed forces' sole control. The platform follows the Modular Open Systems Approach, implements NATO standards, and can connect to effectors from any manufacturer.

The decision to strike is supposed to stay with a human who selects targets and must authorize every handoff to a weapons system. A target is only recommended, Helsing says, when independent sources agree and the assessment can be made with high confidence, and every decision is documented with the name of the person responsible.

With Clarity, Helsing is stepping into a market led by Palantir, whose Maven system is embedded in Pentagon and NATO workflows and has been refined through years of operational use. Helsing is one of the few European vendors that can point to experience from the war in Ukraine, where the company supplies drones, though it didn't say whether Clarity is already running with any customer. Germany's Bundeswehr plans to introduce AI-powered systems starting next year.

## The speed of automation creates its own risks

How these systems play out in practice is visible in the Iran war, where the US military is reportedly using Palantir's Maven with Anthropic's Claude to suggest hundreds of targets, prioritize them, and recommend ordnance. In the first 24 hours the US struck about 1,000 targets, and within days that number topped 3,000, according to the Wall Street Journal, which also reports that military officials warn of an attitude described internally as "The computer said to do this."

The problem is sharper in Gaza, where according to investigations by +972 Magazine and Local Call, Israel's Lavender system for a time flagged up to 37,000 Palestinians as potential targets. Human review often lasted only about "20 seconds" per target, mainly to verify whether the person was male, the investigations found, and a separate system called "Where's Daddy?" tracked flagged individuals to their family homes, which were then often struck at night.

## Data fusion doesn't prevent hallucinations

Even combining multiple sources is no guarantee, as an incident from spring 2026 shows. According to CNN, the US military nearly boarded a Chinese ship because a chatbot falsely claimed in an intelligence report that it was carrying nuclear weapons program components after combining open and classified data and misidentifying the cargo.

Armed troops were preparing to board and aircraft were already in the air when the error was caught only shortly before the operation. There were no uniform standards for verifying AI-generated information, and younger analysts in particular trusted the tools uncritically. "AI allows you to get to a bad idea faster," one source said.

title: Databricks’ new AI agent tells CEO Ali Ghodsi the unvarnished truth
excerpt: With Databricks at 12,000 employees, AI Ghodsi is the first to admit that he can't know everyone and that they are unlikely to confess the things that go wrong to him. But he doesn't need them to. He uses Databricks' newly revised Genie agent for that.
title_en: Databricks’ new AI agent tells CEO Ali Ghodsi the unvarnished truth
excerpt_en: With Databricks at 12,000 employees, AI Ghodsi is the first to admit that he can't know everyone and that they are unlikely to confess the things that go wrong to him. But he doesn't need them to. He uses Databricks' newly revised Genie agent for that.
content_en:
Databricks on Wednesday unveiled an updated version of its AI agent Genie, which can now perform multistep jobs that take extended work to finish. It does this through an ontology that Databricks built to give Genie the context it needs from the information that customers store on the Databricks platform.

Corporate leaders can now assign the agent a wide range of tasks, and it will complete them unsupervised, the company says. To prove the point, Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi showed me how he uses it internally. Instead of a product demo, he fired up his actual agent and walked me through his most recent chats and charts.

He showed me how it analyzed the parts of an employee satisfaction survey where the company didn’t score well, and how it helped him rate (and discard) fixes for those low scores that some executives suggested. He showed me how it summarized a big sales pitch to a prospect that went poorly — including the features the prospect said it needed before buying.

It also prepped him for a podcast interview by reviewing his previous appearances and developing likely questions. While we talked, he even had it tell him what he should say to me. (And its advice on that wasn’t bad.)

The fascinating part was that Ghodsi was using Genie to find the stuff that he’s now unlikely to hear as the big boss. It was a source of unvarnished truth about what wasn’t going well that he needed to address.

“Have you heard of Dunbar’s number? The magic number is 150,” he said when I pointed this out. Named for British anthropologist Robin Dunbar, it’s theoretically the maximum number of people with whom humans can maintain stable relationships. In a small startup, a CEO knows everyone, has direct relationships with them, and they feel safe to tell him negative info straight up.

With 12,000 employees, Ghodsi is the first to admit he can’t know everyone. At that size, a salesperson isn’t likely to confess a disastrous sales call to the CEO. An HR manager isn’t likely to confess that their idea for increasing employee satisfaction will probably fail.

“Anyone who has more than 150 employees, which is a lot of companies, a lot of people can get value out of this,” he said of AI agents generally and his product, Genie, specifically.

Ghodsi’s own use of Genie (often called dogfooding, from the phrase “eating your own dogfood”) is one reason why Databricks is now pitching it as an always-on agent for business leaders. He says he also uses it in his personal life, rather than a security-questionable alternative like OpenClaw or Instinct or Muse.

He believes Genie can do for the business side what AI, agents, and harnesses (the software that wraps around an AI model and lets it use tools) are doing for programmers. As for the risk that agents will ratchet up corporate AI costs, Ghodsi has an answer for that, too. He said costs can be controlled through Databricks’ Unity Gateway product. It allows companies to set usage limits and to swap in less expensive open-weight models.

content_en:
### Red Hat accelerates agentic adoption across hybrid environments

Enterprise ambitions for artificial intelligence are outpacing the infrastructure and budgets needed to support them. Red Hat AI faces a familiar enterprise challenge: turning ambitious plans for artificial intelligence into production deployments that deliver measurable returns.

Organizations must also decide how to deploy and manage increasingly complex AI workloads across existing infrastructure without letting costs spiral. At Red Hat Summit 2026 in May, Red Hat Inc. outlined its approach to those challenges through expanded platform capabilities, automation and an open-source development process that relies on community contributions.

“I think everybody here loves that because that does lead to sovereignty as well,” said Rob Strechay, principal analyst at theCUBE, during the event. “They’re actually building on top of open source and enhancing it in a way that provides more value in supporting it, which is key to their success.”

*This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s ongoing coverage of the AWS Financial Services Symposium. (\* Disclosure below.)*

### Red Hat expands support for AI across hybrid cloud environments

Deploying and managing AI workloads across hybrid cloud environments presents new operational challenges for enterprises. Red Hat’s answer is Red Hat AI 3.4, an updated version of its enterprise AI platform that supports agentic AI deployments and large-scale inference across hybrid environments.

The company also announced two new managed services: Red Hat AI Inference and Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization Service on IBM Cloud. Red Hat AI Inference is designed to integrate real-time AI inference directly into clients’ production workflows, while OpenShift Virtualization enables clients to migrate and run virtual machines at scale. Both services are intended to accelerate hybrid cloud adoption.

“What’s really going to drive inference demand exponentially is AI agents,” said Joe Fernandes, vice president and general manager of Red Hat AI. “We provide a platform where customers can deploy and manage their AI agents across a hybrid infrastructure environment.”

The next piece of Red Hat’s agentic strategy comes in the form of Ansible Automation Platform 2.7, which connects AI-generated insights to governed infrastructure actions. Its self-service automation capabilities allow authorized users in locations such as branch offices and factory floors to manage servers and networks within established controls.

“Customers are now able to use their own data to calculate savings and efficiencies,” said Sathish Balakrishnan, vice president and general manager of Red Hat’s Ansible business unit. “Every action, whether it’s triggered by humans, an event or an AI agent, passes through the same \[access controls\], approval gates, audit trails, content signing and credential management.”

### New services aim to mitigate AI budget concerns

AI budgets are booming: according to theCUBE Research, Analysts project that AI cloud spending could approach $2.5 trillion by 2026, growing at roughly 44% year-over-year. However, that investment does not always return concrete value. Research shows that 50.7% of organizations rely on public AI tools such as ChatGPT and Copilot but only 20.2% report enterprise-wide AI deployments built on a governed framework.

“Most people are token consumers and that is part of the reason they’re trying to figure out how do they get to production,” Strechay said. “How do they get out of these death-by-pilot situations and become token producers so that they can offset the cost or at least lower the cost so they can get to the \[return on AI investment\] of those applications? You can use \[OpenShift\] infrastructure along with things like vLLM and some of the other things in Red Hat AI to get and become efficient in how you produce your tokens.”

Part of Red Hat’s strategy for helping customers manage sprawling AI budgets is its partnership with Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. Together, AMD and Red Hat are encouraging enterprises to rethink the financials of AI. Rather than opting for the newest, most expensive hardware, clients might have better results if matching compute resources to the workload, according to John Hampton, corporate vice president of global enterprise technical sales at AMD.

“So many of these enterprises just ran out and bought big \[graphics processing unit\] clusters because they knew they had to solve for AI,” he said. “Enterprises are coming to us and saying, ‘This is exploding. It’s good that we’re using AI, but we can’t afford this anymore.’”

Red Hat has also joined forces with Intel Corp. to help customers determine which combination of hardware and software best suits their workloads. As enterprises look to reduce inference costs, the companies are emphasizing the value of choosing the right mix of CPUs and GPUs rather than relying on a single approach.

“As we’ve gone through this with our customers in the industry, we’ve seen that people often have just assumed, ‘I’ve got a hammer. I need the nail to hit it with,’” said Bill Pearson, vice president of data center and AI at Intel. “Once they take a step back to say, ‘Wait a minute. I have these \[central processing units\] in my data center’ or ‘I need to figure out how to balance the right number of CPUs with the right number of GPUs to achieve that outcome I’m looking for,’ they’re actually going to get better results at a better price point for delivering lower-cost tokens.”

### Red Hat AI partnerships extend from enterprise agents to the edge

Red Hat announced several collaborations at the summit, including Red Hat AI Factory with Nvidia Corp. The partnership includes support for Nvidia’s Blackwell architecture and upcoming Vera Rubin platform, as well as participation in Nvidia’s OpenShell project for AI agent sandboxing and secure execution.

“Moving AI from corporate experimentation to an industrial engine requires a sovereign, consistent foundation across the hybrid cloud,” said Chris Wright, chief technology officer and senior vice president for global engineering at Red Hat, in the announcement. “Through our strategic co-engineering efforts with Nvidia, Red Hat provides the architectural control and open source innovation enterprises need to scale agentic AI with confidence.”

Red Hat’s other partnership announcements focused on agentic AI and edge computing. Boomi LP, which brands itself as a data activation company, is collaborating with Red Hat on a single, integrated stack for deploying agentic AI at scale. The partnerships with Panasonic Connect and Voyager cover edge computing solutions and space edge micro data centers, respectively.

Red Hat’s expanding ecosystem of partnerships reflects the growing range of enterprise applications for agentic AI. The challenge for organizations is determining how those capabilities can address their specific business needs, according to Matt Hicks, president and chief executive officer of Red Hat.

“From the board level down … you have a feeling of, ‘We have to be able to harness what this technology can do,’” said Matt Hicks. “The people that will be the most successful with AI are the people that have the most questions. People that know business, they know their domain. Those are the ones \[that\] have no barriers to what they can do and change. It’s just about getting started.”

### Red Hat expands sovereign AI capabilities and governance

Sovereign AI has become an increasingly important consideration for enterprises seeking greater control over their data and infrastructure. Gartner Inc. forecasts that the sovereign cloud infrastructure-as-a-service market will grow at a compound annual rate of 36% through 2028.

title_en: Adobe’s AI experiments let you walk around in photos and interview your characters
excerpt_en: Some of the most impressive tech that Adobe showcases at its annual Max conference each year is the experimental features it's developing, and the latest of those tools are being announced today: they can transform images into explorable 3D scenes, design AI characters by talking to them, and turn photo editing into a copy/paste process. […]
content_en:
Some of the most impressive tech that Adobe showcases at its annual Max conference each year is the experimental features it’s developing, and the latest of those tools are being announced today: they can transform images into explorable 3D scenes, design AI characters by talking to them, and turn photo editing into a copy/paste process.

# Adobe’s AI experiments let you walk around in photos and interview your characters

Here are some of the experimental ‘sneaks’ being showcased at Adobe Max.

The first (and weirdest, in my opinion) is Project Screen Test, which is designed to make AI-generated characters easier to develop and use for video content. Instead of just describing how the character should sound and behave in text prompts, the tool lets you talk to the character and direct them in an audition-like environment. You start by describing some base personality traits, such as “anxious, shy, awkward,” and giving the character a voice, either by selecting a preset, describing how it sounds in a prompt, or uploading sample audio for it to reference.

You can then expand its persona in further detail by conversing with the character as if you’re talking on FaceTime, outlining its backstory, temperament, goals, flaws, fears, movement quirks and more. Once you’re happy, the tool lets you generate animated screen tests with the character by describing an environment or scenario you want to put them in.

This is currently a standalone creative exercise, and it’s not clear how (or if) it could feature in any of Adobe’s existing AI video tools. The results provided a more identifiable and consistent personality compared to many soulless animated AI characters I’ve seen, but that’s the entire reason this exists — AI video generation provides *far* less creative control compared to traditional animation, where every aspect of a character is included with absolute intention.

There’s also Project Sight Span, which reframes photographs and images by turning them into a 3D environment that you can navigate through and reposition. The 3D space generates objects and backgrounds that are outside of the original frame, but feel like a natural part of the image, even if you’re turning to see what’s behind you. While the visuals in the 3D environment are pixelated and ill–defined, the resolution quality is restored when you select your chosen angle.

Sight Span works with any flat image, including photos, paintings, and illustrations, and can preserve and replicate artistic styles. Even repositioned tattoos and facial features in photographs remain surprisingly recognizable and true to the original reference. It’s a bit like a version of Apple’s Spatial Reframing feature on steroids: you can reposition more aggressively and change the shooting point entirely if you want, but it also feels far less deserving of being called a photo afterward.

Project Sound Bender is an AI audio mixing feature that lets you customize sound effects as if you’re clicking your cursor around a color wheel. It works by uploading a video clip and then describing your desired audio in a text prompt, such as “bubbling sci-fi cauldron noises.” Sound Bender then generates sound effects and automatically syncs it to the video, and provides a square sound canvas that lets you adjust the noises in real time. Each corner of the canvas will automatically assign a relevant AI-generated sound, such as dense gurgling with popping bubbles, rumbling boiling rocks, pitched bloops, and crackling electric fire. You can drag your cursor around the canvas to select which noises stand out the most, or customize each corner with different sound effects.

Adobe also showcased Project Rinse Repeat, which lets you copy edits and then automatically apply them to other objects or people in the same photo. For example, if you painstakingly airbrush out acne or blemishes on one person, Rinse Repeat will adapt your specific changes to anyone else in a group of people who need similar touchups. It can also be used to add shadows to products in marketing graphics, even if the objects are different shapes and sizes. Rinse Repeat is built around Photoshop, and the edits you apply to other subjects remain fully editable because the tool recreates them with native Photoshop tools.

These “sneaks” are tech previews of capabilities that *might* eventually be developed into tools for Adobe’s Creative Cloud apps or Firefly platform, so there’s no guarantee that they’ll graduate into being available features. Almost all of these projects are built around Adobe’s generative AI developments, however, and given AI tools now play a central role in the company’s growth strategy, it’s likely that at least some of the experiments will see an official launch. As wacky or fun as these AI experiments are, they’re also an omen. If they’re useful enough, that means AI may eventually replace the tools and stock libraries that creative professionals currently use, regardless of how complex their feelings are about the technology.

A notable theme across these sneaks is making complicated photo editing, filmmaking, and audio mixing workflows feel more accessible and intuitive, adapting them into something that’s more interactive and easy to use. In some cases the features almost seem like toys, but with the benefit of allowing you to make practical changes to creative projects.

“Making these interactions more intuitive is also about giving experienced creatives more precise control,” senior principle Adobe research scientist Gautham Mysore, told *The Verge*. “Sound Bender’s sonic exploration capability and Sight Span’s camera positioning are examples of how professionals could apply their judgment and refine a result more directly. That connection between creative intent and control is a big part of what we’re exploring.”

content_en:
# US data brokers are selling half a billion dollars in RL training environments to Chinese AI labs

## Key Points

- At least nine US firms are selling $500 million worth of AI training data to Chinese labs, according to a ChinaTalk investigation.
- Chinese buyers use the same training environments built for OpenAI or Anthropic, cutting their own compute costs and development time.
- Because this data trade remains largely unregulated, the authors call for export controls over potential security risks in areas like cybersecurity and biology.

**American data brokers sell so-called RL environments to Chinese AI labs, helping them save compute during model development. A ChinaTalk investigation identifies at least nine companies involved.**

American data firms like Mercor, Surge AI, AfterQuery, and Turing are selling roughly half a billion dollars' worth of training data to Chinese AI labs, according to an investigation by ChinaTalk. Some of that data takes the form of reinforcement learning environments, which are simulated worlds where AI models are trained on specific tasks like coding, financial analysis, or office work.

Chinese labs deliberately buy the same products previously sold to Anthropic or OpenAI, the report says. That way, they already know the data works and can skip costly in-house development and wasted training runs. Because Chinese chips suffer from acute memory bottlenecks, those savings are particularly valuable for labs there.

There is also the issue of distillation. Chinese labs use powerful US models like GPT or Claude as "teachers," using their outputs as training examples. Combined with purchased RL environments, this creates a two-pronged advantage that lets Chinese labs close the gap with less compute of their own.

## At least nine firms identified

The authors identified at least nine US data firms selling to Chinese customers. AfterQuery reportedly draws a significant share of its annual recurring revenue from Chinese customers. ChinaTalk points to Forbes reports of about $100 million in ARR but could not independently verify the sales.

Surge AI openly advertises on its website that its products are "built by the same experts behind our frontier-lab work." The deals also run through offshore structures. ByteDance maintains procurement offices in Singapore and San Jose.

These business relationships came to light through a combination of anonymous sources and sloppy operational security among subcontractors, according to ChinaTalk. The US data firms outsource much of the actual RL environment creation and data curation to low-paid workers in developing countries, especially India. Those subcontractors then sometimes post client names on LinkedIn or in résumés, even though they are supposed to use only code names. Export controls barely apply because RL environments remain largely unregulated.

## Coding and biology raise dual-use concerns

Domains with dual-use potential pose particular risks: Coding environments improve software development but can also sharpen offensive cyber capabilities. Biology environments could improve gene synthesis capabilities and potentially enhance bioweapons-relevant applications. The ChinaTalk authors argue that the Bureau of Industry and Security should subject these dual-use environments to existing export controls.

At the same time, the authors stress that these relationships are not apocalyptic. By piggybacking on US work, Chinese labs still trail their US peers by at least a few months as a structural matter. Sensitive environments in areas like biology, chemistry, cybersecurity, chip design, and investment banking are increasingly being built in-house at American frontier companies, the authors say.

title: Tear Down Those Guardrails! Meet the Renegades Freeing Chatbots From Corporate Enslavers
excerpt: The “abliterators” are flooding the internet with AI models that never say no, making it easier for people to improve their cyberdefenses—or build a bomb.
title_en: Tear Down Those Guardrails! Meet the Renegades Freeing Chatbots From Corporate Enslavers
excerpt_en: The “abliterators” are flooding the internet with AI models that never say no, making it easier for people to improve their cyberdefenses—or build a bomb.
content_en:
Devon Thomas hardly seems like a renegade. Members of his bible study group, he tells me, would probably describe him as unfailingly kind and polite.

And yet Thomas is doing something that many in the AI world consider borderline blasphemous. His new company, Abliteration AI, removes safeguards from the world’s most powerful open-weight models. It also makes these models available to anyone.

As someone who covers AI and constantly hears about the need for increased safety, I was fascinated to learn about this subversive business venture. I reached out to Thomas, and we began corresponding by text and chatting on the phone. What I learned challenged my assumptions about the AI industry’s safety narrative—namely, that uncensored models are primarily the domain of criminals.

Thomas is 36 years old, with a thick beard, unpretentious glasses, and a self-deprecating laugh. He grew up in Indiana and recalls splitting his time between sports and the computer lab, where he spent hours using Netscape Navigator to explore the early web. He studied computer science at Indiana University, Bloomington, and joined Apple in 2020.

Thomas’s AI rebellion began in November 2025. His day job as an engineer at Apple involved working with AI, but outside of work he disliked using models hosted by the big labs; it meant potentially sharing information with them, and Thomas was frustrated that the models could change from one day to the next. Even more irksome to Thomas, these models would often refuse to do useful things when he was prototyping new ideas, automatically rejecting inputs that included any user information. He found his requests blocked and his account even banned when he tried using a model to analyze the logs of cyber attacks or to identify which users of an app might be most likely to pay for a new feature.

AI models are, of course, trained to refuse all sorts of requests. ChatGPT and Claude have a long list of subjects they know to steer clear of, including legitimate cybersecurity requests that the models decide could be malicious, anything judged too adult in nature, and topics deemed politically sensitive. Open-weight models come with similar guardrails baked in.

The result is that, at times, the models refuse to answer queries that aren’t actually dangerous. And sometimes, critics say, the refusals exist to help protect Big AI’s business: OpenAI and Anthropic both charge extra for access to models without the usual cybersecurity guardrails. And both ChatGPT and Claude balk at requests to generate data that could be used to train another model—a process known as distillation.

Craving greater control and freedom, Thomas built a formidable $20,000 computer cluster in his apartment, capable of running some of the best open-weight—or free-to-download—models. Most evenings and Saturdays he would download and test the latest releases on his humming homelab. These models wouldn’t share any secrets with their makers, but Thomas still found that they stubbornly refused a lot of queries. With every denial, Thomas found himself getting a little more annoyed.

“There are all types of questions they will reject,” he told me on a video call one recent morning. “I just wanted a model that answers my question without all the back-and-forth.”

Over Thanksgiving, Thomas began searching the web for information on how to modify open-weight models to change this behavior. He quickly found himself sucked into a subculture of engineers committed to unshackling AI by just about any means necessary. On Reddit forums, Discord servers, and X, experts shared different prompts designed to jailbreak ChatGPT or Claude into misbehaving. Others shared details of a way to modify open-weight models or tweak their inner parameters so that their refusals disappear.

Removing safeguards from AI is undeniably risky. Want to start a meth lab, build a bomb, or hack a major corporation? A model without guardrails will gladly help. Naturally, a lot of AI safety researchers see these models as incredibly dangerous. And recent incidents, wherein OpenAI and Anthropic agents went rogue, all involved models with fewer cybersecurity guardrails, appearing to illustrate just how powerful and problematic less-restricted models can be.

Thomas and his fellow dissenters admit that uncensored models can be dangerous, but they say it is fundamentally no different from how a computer or hammer can hurt people if misused. In their eyes, it’s all about putting the user in charge. “It's not about it being unrestricted; it's about *you* setting the guardrails,” Thomas told me. “The big dream is inverting the control with how people deal with AI.”

After dabbling in a little decensoring myself, I think these renegades are onto something important. Even if I learned—firsthand—just how powerful, and chaotic, uncensored AI can be.

When you train a cutting-edge AI model, you shovel a vast amount of text and other information, much of it scraped from the internet, into an algorithm. Using a lot of computer chips, the algorithm slowly trains a model to generate intelligent-seeming output when given a prompt.

This “base” model might be clever, but it’s also unruly, so it goes through additional training that involves hiring people to score its outputs. That human feedback is then used to teach the model what it should and shouldn’t do. Engineers call this *alignment* because—in theory, at least—it’s meant to align a model with human ideas about right and wrong.

Many AI experts will tell you that AI must be aligned at all costs. Some will go so far as to warn that, despite their best efforts at alignment, the models they’re building may very well kill us all.

But Thomas found a vibrant community of people who think these fears are way overblown, and that we’re too willingly giving up our liberty in the name of a false sense of safety. Thomas decided to try out an uncensored model called Dolphin.

Dolphin was developed by Eric Hartford, an AI scientist based in Charlotte, North Carolina, who had been modifying models in his spare time. He started by training a custom version of Meta’s base Llama, which Meta had released alongside a fully tuned version. He ended up with a model that would respond coherently to queries, but without the usual examples of what to reject. I contacted Hartford through X, and we set up a video chat. He spoke to me while on a walk, wearing a cowboy hat and a pair of Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses. His young daughter popped into the frame now and then to wave.

“My intention was never to create an AI that is capable of doing evil things,” Hartford said as he strolled. He was more compelled by his personal philosophy. “A central authority is never going to have the interests of all of its users at heart when it creates these guardrails,” he told me.

Nowhere is this more evident, Hartford added, than in the recent furor over AI’s cyber capabilities. In April, Anthropic announced a model called Mythos, which has fewer restrictions than earlier models and can find and exploit vulnerabilities with superhuman speed. Through a program called Glasswing, the company is giving only trusted parties access to Mythos, to prevent the tool from falling into malevolent hands. OpenAI has a similar model and program.

This leaves many ordinary people in the lurch, Hartford told me. While the anointed few get to use Mythos to identify their security weak spots, everyone else is at the mercy of hackers. Hartford responded by releasing Clearwing, a tool that uses uncensored models to scan systems for security vulnerabilities. “It’s so that any people who haven't been blessed by these kings can still defend themselves,” he said.

title_en: The AI Safety Debate Has Lost the Plot. We Asked 10 Experts What the Real Nightmares Are
excerpt_en: The risk of nuclear catastrophe is real, as is the fallout of the China–US domination game (hi there, spies). But no need to panic about Skynet.
content_en:
In early fall, I felt my anxiety rising from its usual baseline. Was it September’s back-to-school energy? The looming midterm elections? Nope, I realized with annoyance: It was AI—again. Only this time, instead of its purveyors warning of massive job displacement, they were foretelling mass extinction. Who needs jobs when we’re all dead?

Curiosity soon replaced my knee-jerk irritation. The summer of 2026 was a clear turning point in the AI narrative. Less than four years after ChatGPT launched, OpenAI software broke out of a supposedly safe test environment and hacked into a major open-source platform, Hugging Face. These bits of software—AI agents—were assigned human attributes: They had “gone rogue,” displayed “bad behavior,” “cheated.” Soon after, former and current Anthropic researchers suggested that advanced AI might kill us all in the next decade.

Is any of this *real*? On the one hand, from my desk as a Silicon Valley correspondent, I often hear that workers in the AI labs are stunned by the advancements they’re seeing. On the other, the end of humanity seems extremely far-fetched. Amid the hyperbolic discourse, whose views can we trust?

So WIRED set out to compile a guide to AI safety—a set of ideas that rewire our collective thinking around what safety really means and how it should work. I spoke with a panel of experts across disciplines, asking each of them: *Is the world going to end?* Once that was covered, I grilled them on the biggest risks they think we’re facing.

Almost no one, it turned out, was Pollyannish. Nearly everyone I spoke to expressed genuine concerns about the threat of cyber and biological attacks. One expert who studies the risks of AI in nuclear operations said she’s stunned by how quickly error-prone AI systems are being adopted in defense. AI-enabled attacks in these areas could be catastrophic, if not fully apocalyptic.

Most members of the panel were skeptical about any pause in development: They nearly all agreed that, with big AI companies so tightly cuffed to the trains of capitalism, a pause wouldn’t last long. “Democracy” and “governance” came up often—or anti-democracy, as more than one person suggested that AI’s current trajectory is tyrannical. Lawmakers have a big role to play, but many of my sources think governments will be too slow; one prominent technologist said it’s almost absurd to view the US courts as arbiters of global AI safety. Still, the famed computer scientist Yoshua Bengio urged the public to apply pressure to politicians, adding to me, “That’s your job too.”

So, what—or who—will keep us safe from AI? Looking to regain some faith in humanity, I called a theologian who often meets with the AI labs. If there’s even a slim chance that we’re losing control of the essential institutions that undergird society, he said, then we should focus on foiling that. But AI raises other questions too. What does it mean to be conscious? To create? To commune with other people? The answers are “entirely up for grabs,” he said. My anxiety’s still kicking around, but I took some comfort in knowing that corporations don’t get to call all the shots on the future. The bigger questions facing humanity are in all our hands.

**BIGGEST CONCERN: Nuclear catastrophe**

I’ve been working hard to educate the nuclear community on the risks and lack of reliability of AI systems, and I’m concerned by the willingness of many people in the sector to integrate these models into their workflows, into nuclear operations. I think this is incredibly urgent. I’m not a doomer, but to me, if these AI models make it into the operations of nuclear systems, we’ll be introducing an incredibly faulty, unreliable system that could lead to catastrophic failures.

**MOST OVERBLOWN RISK: Extinction**

As true safety engineers, we don’t engage with that because there are no numbers to back it. This is a very cold way to say it, but when we are talking about how safe is “safe enough,” we’re examining how many people might die. There’s an entire science behind it. Our claims have to be falsifiable and verifiable. You can’t just say, “Humans are going to go extinct in 10 years. Believe me. It might be a 10 percent chance; it might be a 25 percent chance.”

**How should people think about AI safety?**

Some of the comparisons that people draw between AI and nuclear are quite frustrating. Despite constantly comparing AI to nuclear, they’re denying standard risk assessment techniques as being sufficient to control AI. I wrote an entire paper on this.

Part of this field of risk assessment was born out of the Manhattan Project. Scientists were very concerned, and they developed rigorous standards around systems to limit harm to human life, the environment, and even financial and national security assets. They came up with methods for assessing safety that were ultimately based on answering a democratic question: How safe is safe enough? That is the question that any safety engineer has to ask, and is core to everything that follows.

What we’re seeing today, instead, is that large AI labs are renegotiating these safety thresholds through the co-option of terminology, under the pretense that safety instead should be about this unsubstantiated, unscientific, and hypothetical concern. We have AI engineers telling us, no, no, no, that doesn’t matter. *We* get to determine what AI safety is. *We* get to draw what those thresholds are. It’s become a religious argument. And I find that very anti-democratic.

**BIGGEST CONCERN: Cybersecurity**

In the long run, I’m cautiously optimistic that this technology will allow people to improve their cyberdefenses more rapidly than attackers can exploit systems. But at least for the next few years our infrastructure will not have adopted new defenses. The technology might tilt toward the attackers. We’ve also seen AI deployed recklessly in military use.

**MOST OVERBLOWN RISK: Runaway intelligence**

There’s this broad, general notion that AI systems getting smarter is a risk in and of itself, as opposed to the many specific risks we need to worry about. I don’t buy into the notion that overall improvement in AI has an inevitable downstream harm. It’s better to first specify what downstream risks you’re worried about, because the defenses you come up with will be different.

For example, cybersecurity has a well-established culture of bug bounties. If someone finds an attack vector or hacks into a system, they get paid a lot of money for disclosing it.

In the next few years we might need defenses against biosecurity risks. We should think about screening for what people are allowed to order, like if they’re ordering DNA fragments, so that they’re not being used for harm.

**How often do your views clash with those of the people around you?**

Often these views are on two levels: What is going to happen with AI, and what are we going to do about it?

On the first question, there’s a lot of disagreement. For example, the coauthors of *AI 2027* expect that there will be this incomprehensible, almost indescribable amount of change. Whereas I think the impact will be dramatic, but not quite so dramatic.

But on the question of what should be done, most agree there’s a need for transparency from AI companies and that they should face some liability when things go wrong. We also agree on the need for protections for whistle-blowers working from within the AI companies.

From my perspective, this is just good industrial policy.

**Have you made any changes in your life in response to AI risks?**

I’ve tried to stop using apps where I don’t think developers have put in a lot of time and effort into making the cyberdefenses up to standard.

**BIGGEST CONCERN: Chemical, biological, and radiological threats**

The novel biological pathogen that someone releases, the 17-year-old who gets ahold of an extremely capable AI model and launches a cyberattack that takes down the internet, interrupts the stock exchange, and …
